claim: HSUR2 is a viral non-coding RNA (ncRNA) that functions as a microRNA (miRNA) adaptor.
source: HSUR2 is a viral non-coding RNA (ncRNA) that functions as a microRNA (miRNA) adaptor.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about HSUR2.

claim: HSUR2 inhibits apoptosis in infected cells by recruiting host miRNAs miR-142–3p and miR-16 to mRNAs encoding apoptotic factors.
source: HSUR2 inhibits apoptosis in infected cells by recruiting host miRNAs miR-142–3p and miR-16 to mRNAs encoding apoptotic factors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about HSUR2 function.

claim: HSUR2's target recognition mechanism is not understood.
source: HSUR2's target recognition mechanism is not understood.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: It is unknown why HSUR2 utilizes miR-16 to downregulate only a subset of transcripts.
source: It is also unknown why HSUR2 utilizes miR-16 to downregulate only a subset of transcripts.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a knowledge gap.

claim: iRICC is a general method for individual-nucleotide resolution RNA-RNA interaction identification by crosslinking and capture.
source: We developed a general method for individual-nucleotide resolution RNA-RNA interaction identification by crosslinking and capture (iRICC) to identify sequences mediating interactions between HSUR2 and target mRNAs in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a methodological development by the authors.

claim: Mutational analyses confirmed identified HSUR2-mRNA interactions.
source: Mutational analyses confirmed identified HSUR2-mRNA interactions and validated iRICC as a method that confidently determines sequences mediating RNA-RNA interactions in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: iRICC is validated as a method that confidently determines sequences mediating RNA-RNA interactions in vivo.
source: Mutational analyses confirmed identified HSUR2-mRNA interactions and validated iRICC as a method that confidently determines sequences mediating RNA-RNA interactions in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by mutational analyses shown in the manuscript.

claim: HSUR2 does not display a 'seed' region to base-pair with most target mRNAs.
source: We show that HSUR2 does not display a 'seed' region to base-pair with most target mRNAs, but instead uses different regions to interact with different transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: HSUR2 uses different regions to interact with different transcripts.
source: We show that HSUR2 does not display a 'seed' region to base-pair with most target mRNAs, but instead uses different regions to interact with different transcripts.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Versatile mode of interaction via variable base-pairing provides HSUR2 with a mechanism for differential miRNA recruitment.
source: We further demonstrate that this versatile mode of interaction via variable base-pairing provides HSUR2 with a mechanism for differential miRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Herpesvirus saimiri (HVS) is an oncogenic γ-herpesvirus that establishes latent infections in T cells of New World monkeys.
source: Herpesvirus saimiri (HVS) is an oncogenic γ-herpesvirus that establishes latent infections in T cells of New World monkeys (Ensser and Fleckenstein, 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: HVS expresses seven small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) of the Sm-class called HSURs during latency.
source: Herpesvirus saimiri (HVS) is an oncogenic γ-herpesvirus that establishes latent infections in T cells of New World monkeys (Ensser and Fleckenstein, 2005) and expresses seven small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) of the Sm-class called HSURs (Albrecht and Fleckenstein, 1992; Lee et al., 1988; Murthy et al., 1986; Wassarman et al., 1989) during latency.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Functions have only been assigned to HSUR1 and HSUR2.
source: So far, functions have only been assigned to HSUR1 and HSUR2.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: HSUR1 and HSUR2 bind host miRNAs.
source: These two viral snRNAs bind host miRNAs (Cazalla et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: HSUR1 binds with perfect complementarity to the seed region of miR-142–3p.
source: HSUR1 binds with perfect complementarity to the seed region of miR-142–3p, whereas it base-pairs with the seed region and the 3' end of miR-27.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: HSUR1 base-pairs with the seed region and the 3' end of miR-27.
source: HSUR1 binds with perfect complementarity to the seed region of miR-142–3p, whereas it base-pairs with the seed region and the 3' end of miR-27.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Interaction of HSUR1 and miR-27 results in the degradation of miR-27 by an unknown mechanism.
source: Interaction of HSUR1 and miR-27 results in the degradation of this miRNA by an unknown mechanism (Cazalla et al., 2010; Pawlica et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: HSUR2 contains sequences that base-pair with perfect complementarity with the seed regions of miR-142–3p and miR-16 without affecting the abundance or activity of these miRNAs.
source: HSUR2 contains sequences that base-pair with perfect complementarity with the seed regions of miR-142–3p and miR-16 without affecting the abundance or activity of these miRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: HSUR2 functions as a miRNA adaptor that base-pairs with host mRNAs and recruits miR-142–3p and miR-16 to promote destabilization of the target mRNAs.
source: Rather, HSUR2 functions as a miRNA adaptor that base-pairs with host mRNAs and recruits miR-142–3p and miR-16 to promote destabilization of the target mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: HVS utilizes HSUR2 to downregulate expression of several proteins including apoptotic factors in latently infected T cells.
source: HVS utilizes this mechanism to downregulate expression of several proteins including apoptotic factors in latently infected T cells (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Psoralen-dependent crosslinking suggests that HSUR2 base-pairs with target mRNAs.
source: Psoralen-dependent crosslinking suggests that HSUR2 base-pairs with target mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: It has not been determined if base-pairing is required for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
source: Psoralen-dependent crosslinking suggests that HSUR2 base-pairs with target mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017), but it has not been determined if base-pairing is required for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The regions of target mRNAs bound by HSUR2 and the sequences mediating such interactions are not known.
source: Most importantly, the regions of target mRNAs bound by HSUR2 and the sequences mediating such interactions are not known.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: It is unclear why the interaction between HSUR2 and miR-16 is required for destabilization of only a subset of, but not all, target mRNAs.
source: It is also unclear why the interaction between HSUR2 and miR-16 is required for destabilization of only a subset of, but not all, target mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap with a citation.

claim: Small ncRNAs that function as guides for the recruitment of effector complexes to target RNAs usually use a specific subregion, or seed sequence to interact with the target transcript.
source: Small ncRNAs that function as guides for the recruitment of effector complexes to target RNAs usually use a specific subregion, or seed sequence to interact with the target transcript.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as general knowledge about small ncRNAs.

claim: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), miRNAs, CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), and bacterial Hfq-dependent small RNAs provide examples of different systems in which the folding of the guide RNA into secondary or tertiary structures exposes a defined sequence that is used for binding to the target RNAs.
source: Small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) (Decatur and Fournier, 2003), miRNAs (Bartel, 2018), CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs), and bacterial Hfq-dependent small RNAs (Gorski et al., 2017) provide examples of different systems in which the folding of the guide RNA into secondary or tertiary structures exposes a defined sequence that is used for binding to the target RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Sm-class ncRNAs can use a subregion to interact with rather diverse sequences through distinct arrangements of base pairs.
source: Members of the Sm-class of ncRNAs part from this norm. In some cases, they can use a subregion to interact with rather diverse sequences through distinct arrangements of base pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about Sm-class ncRNAs.

claim: The 5' end of U7 snRNA can interact with a series of similar sequences downstream of histone genes to promote the 3' end processing of histone pre-mRNAs.
source: For example, the 5' end of U7 snRNA can interact with a series of similar sequences downstream of histone genes to promote the 3' end processing of histone pre-mRNAs (Cotten et al., 1988)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: The 5' end of U1 snRNA interacts, through flexible base-pairing, with a highly diverse sequence element that defines the 5' end of introns.
source: whereas the 5' end of U1 snRNA interacts, also through flexible base-pairing, with a highly diverse sequence element that defines the 5' end of introns (Roca and Krainer, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Sm-class RNAs can use different subregions to interact with different RNA-binding partners.
source: Moreover, Sm-class RNAs can use different subregions to interact with different RNA-binding partners.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about Sm-class RNAs.

claim: U2 snRNA utilizes two different subregions to interact with the branch point sequence and U6 snRNA.
source: For example, U2 snRNA utilizes two different subregions to interact with the branch point sequence and U6 snRNA (Nilsen, 1994; Staley and Guthrie, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The characteristic flexibility of Sm-class RNAs in both the use of subregions for interactions with target RNA transcripts and in the arrangement of base pairs undercuts efforts to predict potential binding sites for HSUR2 in target mRNAs.
source: This characteristic flexibility of Sm-class RNAs in both the use of subregions for interactions with target RNA transcripts and in the arrangement of base pairs undercuts efforts to predict potential binding sites for HSUR2 in target mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference based on the properties of Sm-class RNAs.

claim: iRICC revealed sequences mediating interactions between HSUR2 and 171 binding sites in 110 target mRNAs without any previous knowledge of the regions of target mRNAs bound by HSUR2 or the binding properties of this viral ncRNA.
source: iRICC was able to reveal sequences mediating interactions between HSUR2 and 171 binding sites in 110 target mRNAs without any previous knowledge of the regions of target mRNAs bound by HSUR2 or the binding properties of this viral ncRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data in Supplementary file 1 and 2.

claim: Similar to U2 snRNA, HSUR2 can use different subregions to interact with different target mRNAs.
source: Similar to U2 snRNA, HSUR2 can use different subregions to interact with different target mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Just like U1 or U7 snRNAs, HSUR2 allows for diverse arrangements of base pairs in its interactions with target mRNAs.
source: Just like U1 or U7 snRNAs, HSUR2 also allows for diverse arrangements of base pairs in its interactions with target mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by data shown in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Mutational analyses confirmed the sequences mediating HSUR2-mRNA interactions, establishing iRICC as a robust method that can be broadly applied to identify functional RNA-RNA interactions in vivo.
source: Mutational analyses confirmed the sequences mediating HSUR2-mRNA interactions, establishing iRICC as a robust method that can be broadly applied to identify functional RNA-RNA interactions in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Base-pairing between HSUR2 and the target mRNA determines the differential recruitment of miR-16 to target mRNAs and its use in HSUR2-mediated mRNA destabilization.
source: Finally, we show that base-pairing between HSUR2 and the target mRNA determines the differential recruitment of miR-16 to target mRNAs and its use in HSUR2-mediated mRNA destabilization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: HSUR2 samples were highly reproducible across biological replicates (R = 0.91–0.94).
source: HSUR2 samples were highly reproducible across biological replicates (R = 0.91–0.94).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a measure of experimental reproducibility.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO)-term enrichment analysis revealed that HSUR2 regulate expression of genes that encode proteins with roles in the regulation of apoptosis and cell cycle progression.
source: Gene Ontology (GO)-term enrichment analysis revealed that HSUR2 regulate expression of genes that encode proteins with roles in the regulation of apoptosis and cell cycle progression, processes that are relevant in herpesviral latency (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by GO-term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: HSUR2 targets include previously identified HSUR2 target mRNAs (e.g. NGDN) and additional mRNAs encoding pro-apoptotic factors (e.g. caspase 3, STK4, IRF1 and Rassf1).
source: Targets include previously identified HSUR2 target mRNAs (e.g. NGDN) (Gorbea et al., 2017) and additional mRNAs encoding pro-apoptotic factors (e.g. caspase 3, STK4, IRF1 and Rassf1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and reference to supplementary data.

claim: Transient knockdown of HSUR2 expression with an antisense oligonucleotide confirmed that iRICC identified functional targets of HSUR2.
source: Transient knockdown of HSUR2 expression with an antisense oligonucleotide (HSUR2 ASO) (Cazalla et al., 2010; Gorbea et al., 2017) confirmed that iRICC identified functional targets of HSUR2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reverse transcriptase elongation is blocked by psoralen-mediated crosslinking of intramolecular and intermolecular RNA-RNA interactions, which results in a steep drop of aligned reads at the site of crosslinking.
source: Reverse transcriptase elongation is blocked by psoralen-mediated crosslinking (Ericson and Wollenzien, 1988) of intramolecular and intermolecular RNA-RNA interactions, which results in a steep drop of aligned reads at the site of crosslinking (Figure 1C,D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a citation and supported by data shown in Figures 1C, 1D, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Base-pairing between HSUR2 and regions of target mRNAs was indicated by a steep drop of reads in most (78%) of the cases, or by the edge of the peak in some (16.5%) cases.
source: Base-pairing between HSUR2 and regions of target mRNAs was indicated by a steep drop of reads in most (78%) of the cases, or by the edge of the peak in some (16.5%) cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: In a few cases (5.5%), a sharp drop of aligned reads occurred at mRNA regions that did not show significant complementarity with HSUR2 and were therefore not considered for further analysis.
source: In a few cases (5.5%), a sharp drop of aligned reads occurred at mRNA regions that did not show significant complementarity with HSUR2 and were therefore not considered for further analysis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of data filtering.

claim: iRICC identified and determined the sequences comprising 171 binding sites for HSUR2 in 110 target mRNAs.
source: iRICC identified and determined the sequences comprising 171 binding sites for HSUR2 in 110 target mRNAs (Supplementary file 1 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Supplementary files 1 and 2.

claim: Psoralen is most reactive with juxtaposed pyrimidines at the end of helical runs or at G-U wobbles.
source: Psoralen is most reactive with juxtaposed pyrimidines at the end of helical runs or at G-U wobbles (Bachellerie and Hearst, 1982; Thompson et al., 1982).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The arrangement of pyrimidines was present within 10 nucleotides of the position marked by the sharp drop of aligned reads in ~89% of the HSUR2-mRNA duplexes identified.
source: This arrangement of pyrimidines was present within 10 nucleotides of the position marked by the sharp drop of aligned reads in ~89% of the HSUR2-mRNA duplexes identified (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), supporting the base-pairing predicted by RNAcofold.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: HSUR2-binding site distribution on mRNAs is reminiscent of that of miRNAs.
source: HSUR2-binding site distribution on mRNAs is reminiscent of that of miRNAs (Chi et al., 2009; Hafner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations supporting the comparison.

claim: HSUR2 binding sites were enriched in the 3′UTRs of target mRNAs (~67%).
source: HSUR2 binding sites were enriched in the 3′UTRs of target mRNAs (~67%, Figure 2A), with a slight preference for positions proximal to stop codons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A substantial (~26%) fraction of HSUR2 binding sites were located in the coding sequence of target mRNAs.
source: A substantial (~26%) fraction of HSUR2 binding sites were located in the coding sequence of target mRNAs, a location where miRNAs can exert regulation (Fang and Rajewsky, 2011; Schnall-Levin et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations supporting the claim that miRNAs can regulate at this location.

claim: A smaller fraction (~6%) of binding sites overlapped with the stop codon.
source: and a smaller fraction (~6%) of binding sites overlapped with the stop codon.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of binding site distribution.

claim: Only a small number (~2%) of binding sites were located in 5′UTRs.
source: Only a small number (~2%) of binding sites were located in 5′UTRs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a description of binding site distribution.

claim: Most HSUR2 target mRNAs (~58%) contain one HSUR2 binding site.
source: Most HSUR2 target mRNAs (~58%) contain one HSUR2 binding site, with smaller subsets of target mRNAs containing up to five bindings sites (Figure 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Several molecules of HSUR2 can cooperatively repress specific target mRNAs.
source: Most HSUR2 target mRNAs (~58%) contain one HSUR2 binding site, with smaller subsets of target mRNAs containing up to five bindings sites (Figure 2B), suggesting the possibility that, like miRNAs, several molecules of HSUR2 can cooperatively repress specific target mRNAs (Grimson et al., 2007; Saetrom et al., 2007).
evidence: This is suggested in the Results section based on the observation of multiple binding sites and comparison to miRNA behavior, with citations supporting the miRNA cooperative repression.

claim: HSUR2 did not downregulate the expression of firefly luciferase transcripts that lacked a 3′UTR or were fused to the 3′UTR of BCCIP, a gene not targeted by HSUR2.
source: HSUR2 did not downregulate the expression of firefly luciferase transcripts that lacked a 3′UTR or were fused to the 3′UTR of BCCIP, a gene not targeted by HSUR2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), arguing that the firefly luciferase transcript does not contain functional HSUR2 binding sites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HSUR2 repressed to varying extents the expression of all six tested reporter genes carrying partial 3′UTRs of target mRNAs containing single HSUR2 binding sites identified by iRICC.
source: In contrast, HSUR2 repressed to varying extents the expression of all six tested reporter genes carrying partial 3′UTRs of target mRNAs containing single HSUR2 binding sites identified by iRICC (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No repression of luciferase transcripts was observed when a mutant version of HSUR2 that cannot bind miR-142–3p (HSUR2Δ142–3p) was expressed.
source: No repression of luciferase transcripts was observed when a mutant version of HSUR2 that cannot bind miR-142–3p (HSUR2Δ142–3p) and does not repress target mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017) was expressed (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Repression of reporter transcripts occurs through HSUR2-mediated miRNA recruitment.
source: No repression of luciferase transcripts was observed when a mutant version of HSUR2 that cannot bind miR-142–3p (HSUR2Δ142–3p) and does not repress target mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017) was expressed (Figure 3B), indicating that repression of reporter transcripts occurs through HSUR2-mediated miRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HSUR2 did not affect the expression of mutant reporter genes carrying 3′UTRs with point mutations predicted to disrupt interactions with HSUR2.
source: In every case, HSUR2 did not affect the expression of mutant reporter genes carrying 3′UTRs with point mutations predicted to disrupt interactions with HSUR2 (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutant versions of HSUR2 with compensatory mutations predicted to restore complementarity with the corresponding mutant 3′UTR showed similar repressive activity when compared to wild-type HSUR2.
source: Mutant versions of HSUR2 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) with compensatory mutations predicted to restore complementarity with the corresponding mutant 3′UTR in all cases showed similar repressive activity when compared to wild-type HSUR2 (Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Base-pairing between HSUR2 and target mRNAs is required for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
source: Collectively, these results confirm that base-pairing between HSUR2 and target mRNAs is required for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression, and that the interactions are mediated by the sequences identified by iRICC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutational analyses shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The interactions between HSUR2 and target mRNAs are mediated by the sequences identified by iRICC.
source: Collectively, these results confirm that base-pairing between HSUR2 and target mRNAs is required for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression, and that the interactions are mediated by the sequences identified by iRICC.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the mutational analyses shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: HSUR2 could repress both mutant reporters as efficiently as wild-type reporters when mutations resulted in interactions through different base-pairing arrangements while maintaining similar binding stabilities.
source: HSUR2 could repress both mutant reporters as efficiently as wild-type reporters (Figure 3B and Figure 5), indicating that HSUR2 can still bind to the modified sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The stability of the interaction between HSUR2 and its target mRNA, rather than any specific base-pairing arrangement, dictates HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
source: These observations indicate that the stability of the interaction between HSUR2 and its target mRNA, rather than any specific base-pairing arrangement, dictates HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: The miR-16 binding site in HSUR2 (miR-16BS) is directly engaged with the target in ~80% of mRNA interactions.
source: We noticed that the miR-16 binding site in HSUR2 (miR-16BS, Figure 1C) is directly engaged with the target in ~80% of mRNA interactions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Once the miR-16BS is engaged in base-pairing with a target mRNA, HSUR2 can no longer bind to miR-16 and should therefore repress that target mRNA in a miR-16-independent manner.
source: and hypothesized that once the miR-16BS is engaged in base-pairing with a target mRNA, HSUR2 can no longer bind to miR-16 and should therefore repress that target mRNA in a miR-16-independent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a hypothesis based on the observation of miR-16BS engagement.

claim: Inhibition of miR-142–3p activity with locked nucleic acid (LNA) inhibitors ablated HSUR2's ability to repress the expression of all luciferase reporter transcripts tested.
source: As expected, inhibition of miR-142–3p activity with locked nucleic acid (LNA) inhibitors ablated HSUR2's ability to repress the expression of all luciferase reporter transcripts tested (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2) (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Inhibition of miR-16 ablated HSUR2-mediated repression of reporter transcripts carrying partial PACS1, STK4, MGA, and CD69 3′UTRs, all of which are bound by HSUR2 without engaging the miR-16BS.
source: Similarly, inhibition of miR-16 ablated HSUR2-mediated repression of reporter transcripts carrying partial PACS1, STK4, MGA, and CD69 3′UTRs (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C), all of which are bound by HSUR2 without engaging the miR-16BS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Inhibition of miR-16 with an LNA inhibitor did not affect HSUR2's ability to repress luciferase reporter transcripts carrying partial TP53RK and YTHDC1 3′UTRs, both of which contain HSUR2 binding sites that base-pair with the miR-16BS.
source: In contrast, inhibition of miR-16 with an LNA inhibitor did not affect HSUR2's ability to repress luciferase reporter transcripts carrying partial TP53RK and YTHDC1 3′UTRs (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), both of which contain HSUR2 binding sites that base-pair with the miR-16BS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The arrangement of base pairs between HSUR2 and its target mRNA determines the availability of the miR-16BS and therefore dictates whether HSUR2 utilizes this miRNA for mRNA repression.
source: These results suggest that the arrangement of base pairs between HSUR2 and its target mRNA determines the availability of the miR-16BS and therefore dictates whether HSUR2 utilizes this miRNA for mRNA repression (Figure 7).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figure 6, with Figure 7 illustrating the model.

claim: Inhibition of miR-16 activity prevented HSUR2 from repressing the wild-type PACS1 reporter transcript.
source: Inhibition of miR-16 activity prevented HSUR2 from repressing the wild-type PACS1 reporter transcript (Figure 6A) presumably because the miR-16BS is not used to bind PACS1 mRNA
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: miR-16 no longer affected HSUR2's ability to repress the mutant altbsPACS1mut reporter transcript which now interacted with HSUR2 through its miR-16BS.
source: whereas miR-16 no longer affected HSUR2's ability to repress the mutant altbsPACS1mut reporter transcript which now interacted with HSUR2 through its miR-16BS (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: miR-16 activity was not required for HSUR2-mediated repression of the wild-type TP53RK reporter transcript which uses the miR-16BS in its interaction with HSUR2.
source: Conversely, miR-16 activity was not required for HSUR2-mediated repression of the wild-type TP53RK reporter transcript which uses the miR-16BS in its interaction with HSUR2 (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: miR-16 activity was required for repression of the altbsTP53RKmut reporter transcript, which was redesigned to interact with HSUR2 without base-pairing with its miR-16BS.
source: but miR-16 activity was required for repression of the altbsTP53RKmut reporter transcript, which was redesigned to interact with HSUR2 without base-pairing with its miR-16BS (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Base-pairing between HSUR2 and target mRNAs dictates the availability of the miR-16BS and therefore the requirement of miR-16 activity for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
source: These results indicate that base-pairing between HSUR2 and target mRNAs dictates the availability of the miR-16BS and therefore the requirement of miR-16 activity for HSUR2-mediated mRNA repression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Several methods based on psoralen-mediated crosslinking and proximity ligation have been developed recently to identify RNA-RNA interactions.
source: Several methods based on psoralen-mediated crosslinking and proximity ligation have been developed recently to identify RNA-RNA interactions (Aw et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: All psoralen-based proximity ligation methods rely on proximity ligation of psoralen-crosslinked RNAs, high-throughput sequencing, and identification of chimeric reads to infer RNA-RNA interactions.
source: All these methods rely on proximity ligation of psoralen-crosslinked RNAs, high-throughput sequencing, and identification of chimeric reads to infer RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of existing methods.

claim: The requirement for reversal of the psoralen crosslinks before library preparation makes proximity ligation methods unsuitable for determining the nucleotides involved in psoralen-mediated crosslinking.
source: The requirement for reversal of the psoralen crosslinks before library preparation makes these methods unsuitable for determining the nucleotides involved in psoralen-mediated crosslinking and thus cannot distinguish bona fide, in vivo RNA-RNA interactions from RNA duplexes that are generated in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: iRICC relies on psoralen crosslinking-dependent reverse-transcriptase stalling during library preparation to identify sites of crosslinking and to determine the precise sequences involved in base-pairing.
source: This method relies on psoralen crosslinking-dependent reverse-transcriptase stalling during library preparation to identify sites of crosslinking and to determine the precise sequences involved in base-pairing.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a description of the iRICC method.

claim: iRICC defined the sequences mediating interactions between HSUR2 and 171 binding sites in target mRNAs.
source: iRICC defined the sequences mediating interactions between HSUR2 and 171 binding sites in target mRNAs (Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Psoralen derivatives preferably crosslink adjacent opposite pyrimidine bases in double-stranded regions.
source: Since psoralen derivatives preferably crosslink adjacent opposite pyrimidine bases in double-stranded regions (Bachellerie and Hearst, 1982; Cimino et al., 1985; Thompson et al., 1982)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Interactions mediated by GC-rich regions will be under-represented in datasets generated by iRICC.
source: we predict that interactions mediated by GC-rich regions will be under-represented in datasets generated by iRICC.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a prediction based on the properties of psoralen crosslinking.

claim: iRICC successfully identified functional RNA-RNA interactions in vivo.
source: iRICC therefore successfully identified functional RNA-RNA interactions in vivo, providing a reliable and general solution to the long-standing problem of identifying unknown, functional RNA-RNA interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion based on the mutational analyses.

claim: Gene set enrichment analyses of targets identified by iRICC indicated that HSUR2 regulates the expression of genes with roles in processes relevant to viral infection.
source: Gene set enrichment analyses of targets identified by iRICC indicated that HSUR2 regulates the expression of genes with roles in processes relevant to viral infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Supplementary file 4) as previously described (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Only three mRNAs previously described by RICC-seq as targets of HSUR2 were identified by iRICC.
source: However, only three mRNAs previously described by RICC-seq (Gorbea et al., 2017) as targets of HSUR2 were identified by iRICC, suggesting that both techniques underestimate the number of mRNAs targeted by HSUR2.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation from comparing the two methods.

claim: HSUR2's primary function is to deliver miRNAs to mRNAs.
source: HSUR2's primary function is to deliver miRNAs to mRNAs (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: It is not surprising that HSUR2 binding sites are found primarily in 3′UTRs where most miRNA binding sites occur.
source: It is therefore not surprising that HSUR2 binding sites are found primarily in 3′UTRs (Figure 2B) where most miRNA binding sites occur (Chi et al., 2009; Hafner et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim about miRNA binding sites.

claim: The mechanism by which HSUR2 can specifically recognize binding sites in target mRNAs remains unknown.
source: The mechanism by which HSUR2 can specifically recognize binding sites in target mRNAs remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a knowledge gap.

claim: The fact that HSUR2 does not present a specialized or seed region that base-pairs with most binding sites suggests that sequence complementarity is required but not sufficient for the selection of target mRNAs.
source: The fact that HSUR2 does not present a specialized or seed region that base-pairs with most binding sites (see below) suggest that sequence complementarity is required but not sufficient for the selection of target mRNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the data.

claim: Base-pairing between U1 snRNA and the 5' splice site and between U2 snRNA and the branchpoint sequence are essential for splicing.
source: For example, base-pairing between U1 snRNA and the 5' splice site and between U2 snRNA and the branchpoint sequence are essential for splicing (Black et al., 1985; Mount et al., 1983; Parker et al., 1987; Séraphin et al., 1988; Siliciano and Guthrie, 1988; Wu and Manley, 1989; Zhuang and Weiner, 1986; Zhuang and Weiner, 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations supporting the claim.

claim: Cis-acting signals like splicing enhancers, and trans-acting factors like SR proteins are essential for guiding and escorting spliceosomal small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs) to the appropriate splicing signals before base-pairing is established.
source: Yet, cis-acting signals like splicing enhancers, and trans-acting factors like SR proteins are essential for guiding and escorting spliceosomal small nuclear ribonucleoprotein particles (snRNPs) to the appropriate splicing signals before base-pairing is established (Kohtz et al., 1994; Lavigueur et al., 1993; Roscigno and Garcia-Blanco, 1995; Sun et al., 1993; Tarn and Steitz, 1995; Tian and Maniatis, 1993).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The combination of protein-assisted recruitment of snRNPs and RNA-RNA base-pairing results in exquisite specificity as well as enormous regulatory potential, which is manifested by the immense protein diversity that is generated by alternative splicing.
source: This combination of protein-assisted recruitment of snRNPs and RNA-RNA base-pairing results in exquisite specificity as well as a enormous regulatory potential, which is manifested by the immense protein diversity that is generated by alternative splicing (Nilsen and Graveley, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Additional cis- and trans-acting factors may assist HSUR2 in the recognition of binding sites in target mRNAs increasing both the specificity and versatility of HSUR2-mediated mRNA regulation.
source: It is conceivable that, similarly to cellular snRNPs, additional cis- and trans-acting factors may assist HSUR2 in the recognition of binding sites in target mRNAs increasing both the specificity and versatility of HSUR2-mediated mRNA regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on comparison to cellular snRNPs.

claim: HSUR2 can interact with the same target through different arrangement of base pairs.
source: Mutational analyses showed that HSUR2 can interact with the same target through different arrangement of base pairs (Figure 5), pointing to the stability of the interaction as the main variable determining the outcome of HSUR2-mediated mRNA regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The binding properties of HSUR2 confer this viral ncRNA with potential advantages over seed-based systems.
source: We hypothesize that the binding properties of HSUR2 confer this viral ncRNA with potential advantages over seed-based systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: For small regulatory ncRNAs that employ seed-based mechanisms for target regulation, the repertoire of regulated transcripts is constrained by the presence of a discrete sequence complementary to the seed region of the ncRNA.
source: For small regulatory ncRNAs that employ seed-based mechanisms for target regulation, the repertoire of regulated transcripts is constrained by the presence of a discrete sequence complementary to the seed region of the ncRNA, in the same way that the size of a wrench constrains the size of bolts and nuts that can be adjusted with it.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an analogy to explain seed-based regulation.

claim: Most herpesviruses express large numbers of miRNAs to regulate a diverse collection of transcripts during latency to generate a cellular environment that is conducive to viral persistence.
source: By analogy, most herpesviruses express large numbers of miRNAs to regulate a diverse collection of transcripts during latency to generate a cellular environment that is conducive to viral persistence (Skalsky and Cullen, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: Flexible base-pairing allows HSUR2 to regulate a diverse group of transcripts functioning like a 'crescent wrench' that can be adjusted to fit nuts and bolts of different sizes.
source: We propose that flexible base-pairing allows HSUR2 to regulate a diverse group of transcripts functioning like a 'crescent wrench' that can be adjusted to fit nuts and bolts of different sizes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed model using an analogy.

claim: By using ncRNAs that employ 'non-seed' or flexible base-pairing, HVS can potentially minimize the number of regulatory ncRNAs required to effectively regulate a defined set of transcripts and therefore minimize the investment in viral genome space.
source: By using ncRNAs that employ 'non-seed' or flexible base-pairing, HVS can potentially minimize the number of regulatory ncRNAs required to effectively regulate a defined set of transcripts and therefore minimize the investment in viral genome space.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about the evolutionary advantage of HSUR2's binding properties.

claim: Seed-based RNA regulatory systems are sensitive to mismatches in interactions between the seed region of the ncRNA and target transcripts.
source: Seed-based RNA regulatory systems are sensitive to mismatches in interactions between the seed region of the ncRNA and target transcripts (Bartel, 2018; Chipman and Pasquinelli, 2019; Gorski et al., 2017; Künne et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Single mismatches in the seed region of miRNAs can dramatically reduce their association with target transcripts.
source: Single mismatches in the seed region of miRNAs can dramatically reduce their association with target transcripts (Chandradoss et al., 2015; Salomon et al., 2015; Schirle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: Single point mutations in binding sites can render regulation by miRNAs ineffectual, making it relatively easy for the host to escape viral miRNA-based regulation.
source: Thus, single point mutations in binding sites can render regulation by miRNAs ineffectual, making it relatively easy for the host to escape viral miRNA-based regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the sensitivity of seed-based systems to mismatches.

claim: Extensive mutagenesis of HSUR2 binding sites does not affect HSUR2 binding as long as new base pairs are formed to maintain a similar overall binding affinity.
source: We have shown that extensive mutagenesis of HSUR2 binding sites does not affect HSUR2 binding as long as new base pairs are formed to maintain a similar overall binding affinity (Figure 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: HSUR2's binding flexibility allows HSUR2-mediated regulation to withstand considerable target sequence evolution, making it difficult for the host to escape this viral mechanism of gene regulation.
source: We speculate that this binding flexibility allows HSUR2-mediated regulation to withstand considerable target sequence evolution, making it difficult for the host to escape this viral mechanism of gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about the evolutionary advantage of HSUR2's binding properties.

claim: The molecular mechanism through which miR-142–3p contributes to repression of all HSUR2 target mRNAs tested so far is currently unknown.
source: The molecular mechanism through which miR-142–3p contributes to repression of all HSUR2 target mRNAs tested so far is currently unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a knowledge gap.

claim: miR-142-3p is abundantly expressed in hematopoietic tissues and mostly absent in non-hematopoietic ones.
source: Since this miRNA is abundantly expressed in hematopoietic tissues and mostly absent in non-hematopoietic ones (Chen et al., 2004)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: HSUR2 would not be able to repress target mRNAs in non-hematopoietic tissues, curbing the ability of HVS to establish latent infections in non-hematopoietic tissues and thus defining the tropism of this virus' latent infection.
source: it is conceivable that HSUR2 would not be able to repress target mRNAs in non-hematopoietic tissues, curbing the ability of HVS to establish latent infections in non-hematopoietic tissues and thus defining the tropism of this virus' latent infection.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the tissue-specific expression of miR-142-3p.

claim: GO-term enrichment analysis showed that miR-16-dependent HSUR2 targets encode proteins with roles in apoptosis.
source: GO-term enrichment analysis showed that miR-16-dependent HSUR2 targets encode proteins with roles in apoptosis, consistent with the fact that the interaction between miR-16 and HSUR2 is required for inhibition of apoptosis by this viral Sm-class RNA (Gorbea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by GO-term enrichment analysis with a citation.

claim: The miR-16 family regulates the cell cycle by modulating the expression of genes with critical roles in the G1-S transition including cyclins D1, D2, D3, E1, and CDK6.
source: The miR-16 family regulates the cell cycle by modulating the expression of genes with critical roles in the G1-S transition including cyclins D1, D2, D3, E1, and CDK6 (Bonci et al., 2008; Cimmino et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations supporting the claim.

claim: The abundance of members of the miR-16 family is dynamically regulated by the cell cycle, with the highest abundance of these miRNAs observed in cells that are arrested in G0.
source: Interestingly, the abundance of members of this family of miRNAs is dynamically regulated by the cell cycle, with the highest abundance of these miRNAs observed in cells that are arrested in G0 (Rissland et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation supporting the claim.

claim: The abundance of miR-16 family members determines the extent to which HSUR2 can affect its targets.
source: Assuming that the abundance of these miRNAs determines the extent to which HSUR2 can affect its targets, we speculate that this mechanism allows HSUR2 to efficiently repress a subset of transcripts in a cell cycle-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an assumption underlying a speculation.

claim: HSUR2's mechanism allows it to efficiently repress a subset of transcripts in a cell cycle-dependent manner.
source: Assuming that the abundance of these miRNAs determines the extent to which HSUR2 can affect its targets, we speculate that this mechanism allows HSUR2 to efficiently repress a subset of transcripts in a cell cycle-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation.

claim: HSUR2's mechanism provides a way for HVS to regulate the expression of key genes in specific situations, like when the latently infected cell tries to arrest in G0.
source: This provides a mechanism for HVS to regulate the expression of key genes in specific situations, like when the latently infected cell tries to arrest in G0.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation about the biological significance of HSUR2's mechanism.
